sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe patient matching and explain why linking each patient to a single correct record is essential.
- Apply two-identifier verification to confirm patient identity before accessing, disclosing, or changing records.
- Prevent duplicate records through thorough searching, accurate data entry, and controlled merge procedures.
- Explain why duplicate and mismatched records harm patient safety and privacy, and how matching supports HIPAA safeguards.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Patient matching is like making sure every piece of mail about you goes into your mailbox and not your neighbor's — the office checks that the record it is opening really belongs to you.

### Question 2

Just like a password plus a PIN is safer than only one of them, checking two facts about a patient (like name and birthday) makes it much harder to mix two people up.

### Question 3

A room number is like labeling your backpack by which desk you sat at today — it changes all the time and does not really say who you are.

### Question 4

It is like the office asking for your name AND your birthday, so they open your folder and not a folder for someone else with the same name.

### Question 5

A duplicate is like getting a second report card when you already have one, just because someone did not find the first one before starting a new one.

### Question 6

It is like checking every drawer in the house for your keys before assuming they are lost and buying new ones.

### Question 7

If two kids in class are both named Sam, you tell them apart by their birthdays and their different student ID numbers, not by what they are wearing.

### Question 8

It is like writing down someone's birthday wrong because you swapped two numbers — the real birthday did not change, the note was just wrong.

### Question 9

'Jr.' and 'Sr.' are like the different middle names that keep a dad and son who share a name from being mixed up.

### Question 10

It is like looking for a friend in a phone book under 'Garcia-Lopez,' 'Garcia Lopez,' or just 'Lopez' — you have to try a few spellings.

### Question 11

Your official name is the one on your birth certificate, like 'William,' even if everyone calls you 'Bill' — the office keeps the official one and makes a note of the nickname.

### Question 12

A duplicate is having two folders for one person; an overlay is putting one person's papers inside a different person's folder by mistake.

### Question 13

If your allergy note is in one folder but the doctor only looks at the other folder, the doctor might not know about it — that is dangerous.

### Question 14

It is like a puzzle split between two boxes — each box is missing pieces, so you never see the whole picture.

### Question 15

The office put the test result in the wrong person's folder because it only looked at the name and forgot to check the birthday.

### Question 16

If you find two half-filled folders for one person, the right move is to ask a grown-up in charge to carefully combine them, not to throw one away.

### Question 17

The MPI is like the library's master catalog that tells you exactly which shelf each person's book is on so two books are not mixed up.

### Question 18

An MRN is like a library card number that belongs only to you and stays the same no matter how many times you visit.

### Question 19

It is like asking someone to tell you their birthday instead of saying 'your birthday is Tuesday, right?' — people might just say yes even if it is wrong.

### Question 20

It is harder to know who is really on the other end of a phone call because you cannot see them, so extra care is needed.

### Question 21

If you are not sure who is really on the phone, the safe move is to ask a manager for help rather than hand over private information.

### Question 22

When someone gets a new last name, you update their existing folder instead of starting a whole new folder for the same person.

### Question 23

If you open the wrong folder and start reading it out loud, you could share one person's private health information with someone else.

### Question 24

It is like only asking for the one piece of ID you need at the door, instead of asking to see someone's whole wallet.

### Question 25

Your Social Security number is like a master key to your money — you would not hand it out just to check in at a desk.

### Question 26

Even twins who share a birthday have different middle names and different ID numbers — those are what keep their folders apart.

### Question 27

Combining folders is a job for the specially trained people in charge of records, not something anyone at the front desk does on their own.

### Question 28

Spelling someone's name back to them, like double-checking a phone number, catches mistakes while there is still time to fix them.

### Question 29

Writing '03/04' can mean March 4th or April 3rd depending on where you are, so the office agrees on one clear way to write every date.

### Question 30

A middle name is like an extra clue that helps you pick the right 'Jordan Lee' out of two different people with that name.

### Question 31

If something in a folder does not seem to belong to that person, you tell the person in charge instead of ripping pages out yourself.

### Question 32

If you almost put your shoes on the wrong feet, noticing and telling someone can stop it from happening for real next time.

### Question 33

Matching is like putting a name tag on your folder so it stays with you; de-identification is like removing the name tag so no one can tell whose folder it is.

### Question 34

Your real, legal name goes on the official folder; the insurance card name is just a note the billing people use.

### Question 35

Your insurance card number is like a membership card number for a gym — it is yours, but if you switch gyms, you get a new one.

### Question 36

Moving houses means updating the address on your existing folder, not starting a whole new folder.

### Question 37

If the doctor writes your test order on someone else's clipboard, your results could end up in the wrong file and the wrong person could get treated for them.

### Question 38

Matching is how the office makes sure private information about you stays with you and is not given out about the wrong person.

### Question 39

It is like asking to see only the one ID card you need, not someone's entire wallet.

### Question 40

If you are not sure which folder is really the person's, you sort it out first so they get their own papers and not someone else's.

### Question 41

If someone's private health information goes to the wrong person, the office has to look into it and tell the person it happened — it is a serious matter.

### Question 42

It is like a school checking your student ID every day — even if they know you, the check keeps the right person attached to the right record.

### Question 43

The record is the whole folder of everything the office knows about a patient's health, not just one page.

### Question 44

Even when someone says they are new, you peek in the filing cabinet first to be sure there is not already a folder for them.

### Question 45

The important things to write down are the facts that help find you again later: your full name, birthday, and how to reach you.

### Question 46

If two folders look almost exactly alike, you ask for more clues and, if still unsure, ask a manager rather than guessing.

### Question 47

For a child, you check the child's name and birthday and make sure the grown-up with them is allowed to act for them.

### Question 48

You cannot give out someone's private health information just because a caller says they are helping — you need real proof they are allowed.

### Question 49

Before handing over private papers, the office checks that the person picking them up is really the right person.

### Question 50

It means you are allowed to see and get a copy of your own health folder — not anyone else's.

### Question 51

Matching is like making sure the right key opens the right locker — it keeps information going only to where it belongs.

### Question 52

Your login is like your own locker key — if you share it, no one can tell who really opened the locker.

### Question 53

The system is raising its hand to say 'wait, this might already be here' — so you stop and check before making a new one.

### Question 54

If you find two folders for one person right in the middle of a doctor visit, the doctor needs to know right away so they use the right, complete information today.

### Question 55

When you are in a hurry, it is easier to grab the wrong folder by mistake — so the office slows down the important checks even when busy.

### Question 56

Integrity means the information in your folder is right, complete, and really about you.

### Question 57

An encounter is one visit — like one page added to your folder each time you come in, all kept in the same folder.

### Question 58

Making an extra folder 'just in case' leads to two folders for one person, which is confusing and unsafe.

### Question 59

If your bills are split between two envelopes, the company has a harder time keeping track of what you owe.

### Question 60

Even if you have an appointment, the office still checks your name and birthday before opening your folder, to be sure it is the right one.

### Question 61

Writing down which checks you did is like keeping a receipt — it shows later what was verified and when.

### Question 62

The official name on your folder is your real, legal name — like the name on your birth certificate.

### Question 63

'O'Brien' and 'OBrien' look almost the same to people but can look different to a computer, which might not find the existing folder.

### Question 64

Name and birthday are both about the person; a room number is about where they are sitting.

### Question 65

Your address and phone number can change when you move, so they are like a temporary tag, not your permanent ID.

### Question 66

If someone makes several online accounts that are not connected to the same folder, the office might end up with more than one folder for them.

### Question 67

After combining two folders, you make sure the one folder now has everything and nothing important was dropped.

### Question 68

Before adding a paper to a folder, you double-check it is the right folder — that keeps one person's papers out of another person's folder.

### Question 69

Practicing the 'check the name and birthday every time' habit keeps everyone doing it the same safe way.

### Question 70

If a note in your folder is about something that never happened to you, it probably got put in the wrong folder by mistake.

### Question 71

Write the name exactly as it really is, letter by letter, like copying a password carefully.

### Question 72

Matching is what makes sure your private health information stays yours and that your doctor is looking at your information, not someone else's.

### Question 73

If lots of people share a last name, you use more than just the last name to tell them apart.

### Question 74

Your medical record number is like a special code that belongs only to you at that office.

### Question 75

One clue matching is not enough — you check more clues before deciding it is really the same person.

### Question 76

The assistant's job is to check the name and birthday carefully and ask a supervisor when something does not add up.

### Question 77

Right before reading someone their results, double-check it is really their folder — not a folder for someone with the same name.

### Question 78

Before combining two folders, you check several clues and have someone in charge approve it, so two different people are never combined.

### Question 79

Before changing anything in a folder, the office first makes sure the person asking is really that patient.

### Question 80

Lots of people share a name, but the birthday is an extra clue that helps find the right person.

### Question 81

For names with spaces, you try a few different ways of writing them to find the right folder.

### Question 82

Two folders with almost the same name and the same birthday are probably the same person — that is worth checking.

### Question 83

If someone had a different name before, you look for the old folder too and make sure they only have one folder.

### Question 84

If you are not sure a test result really belongs to the person, you stop and check — you do not just hand it over.

### Question 85

One complete folder means the doctor sees everything about you, so nothing important gets missed or mixed up.
